timeline.title: Indian Geological History Timeline
timeline.description: The chronological sequence of major tectonic and geological events that shaped the Indian subcontinent.

cards.details: Formation of the oldest crustal rocks (Peninsular gneisses and granites). Deposition of Dharwar sediments, forming the base complex rich in metallic minerals.
Formation of major sedimentary basins (Purana Rock System). Vindhyan sediments deposited, yielding building stones and diamondiferous deposits.

cards.date: Upper Carboniferous to Jurassic (300 - 150 Million Years)
cards.details: Tectonic sagging formed river basins where massive plant matter accumulated in swampy conditions, forming 98% of India's modern coal reserves.
As the Indian plate passed over the Reunion Hotspot, massive basaltic lava erupted through fissures, covering 500,000 sq km of the Peninsular block.

cards.date: Tertiary to Pleistocene (50 Million - 1 Million Years)
cards.details: Collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates closed the Tethys Sea, folding the Himalayas. The foredeep depression filled with alluvium, forming the Great Plains.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Quick cognitive associations for Indian geological systems.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Chronological Order of Indian Rock Systems
items.phrase: "A. D. C. V. G. D. T. (A Dear Companion Visited Gondwana During Today's Tea)"

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Mineral Association of Rock Systems
items.decryption: Quick match for exams: **Dharwar** is the primary source of **metallic minerals** (iron, manganese, gold); **Gondwana** is the primary source of **coal**.

traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Trap 1: Fossil Presence in Archean Rocks: Archean and Dharwar rock systems are completely unfossiliferous (contain no fossils) because they formed before complex life evolved on Earth. A common trap is matching Dharwar rocks with plant fossils.

Trap 2: Coal type of India: Although coal is associated with Carboniferous systems worldwide, India's Carboniferous rocks are mostly marine and lack coal. 98% of Indian coal belongs to the younger Gondwana system (Permian-Jurassic), and it is mostly non-coking bituminous coal.

Trap 3: Geological Stability: The Himalayas are not stable; they are young, weak, and flexible fold mountains still rising due to ongoing plate collision (seismically active Zone V). In contrast, the Peninsular Block is one of the most stable geological shields on Earth.
Trap 4: Karewa Deposits: Karewas are lacustrine (lake-deposited) silt clays found specifically in the Kashmir valley. They are famous for **Saffron (Zafran) cultivation**, not tea or wheat.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Geological divisions of India, structural dynamics, and rock system classifications.

sections.title: 1. Three Major Geological Divisions of India
sections.content:
Geologically, India is divided into three distinct regions with contrasting structures, rock types, and tectonic behaviors.

The Peninsular Block
  • Characteristics: The oldest, most rigid, and stable block of India. Primarily composed of ancient Archean gneisses and granites.
  • Stability: Has stood as a rigid shield since the Cambrian period, only experiencing minor vertical adjustments and coastal submergences.
The Extra-Peninsula (Himalayas)
  • Characteristics: Young, weak, and flexible geological structure. Formed by sedimentary deposits of the Tethys Sea squeezed between two colliding plates.
  • Tectonics: Active plate collision means the mountains are still rising, characterized by folding, faulting, and high seismicity.

3. The Indo-Gangetic Plains: A deep geological depression (foredeep) formed between the rising Himalayas and the stable Peninsula. It is filled with Pleistocene-to-Recent alluvial deposits brought by the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra river systems. Its alluvium thickness ranges from 1,000 to 2,000 meters, making it the youngest geological region of India.

sections.title: 2. Classification of Indian Rock Systems
sections.content:
The rock systems of India are categorized into four major eras, spanning from the oldest Precambrian base to recent sediments.

Archean and Purana Systems
  • Archean System: Gneisses and Schists forming the basement complex. **Dharwar System** is metamorphosed sedimentary rock containing India's major iron, manganese, copper, and gold deposits.
  • Cuddapah System: Famous for slates, quartzites, and limestone. **Vindhyan System** contains sandstone and diamond mines (Panna, Golconda).
Aryan Rock System (Coal & Volcanics)
  • Gondwana System: Formed in river basins; contains 98% of India's coal reserves. Highly fossiliferous (mainly plant fossils like Glossopteris).
  • Deccan Traps: Basaltic lava flows over 500,000 sq km, formed by fissure eruptions when India passed over the Reunion hotspot. Weathered into fertile **Regur (Black Cotton) soil**.

Comparison of Indian Rock Systems:

Rock System Geological Era Fossil Content Economic Importance & Minerals
Archean / Dharwar Precambrian (Archean) Unfossiliferous Metallic minerals (Iron, Manganese, Gold, Copper)
Cuddapah / Vindhyan Precambrian (Proterozoic) Unfossiliferous / Traces Limestone, sandstone, ornamental stone, diamonds
Gondwana System Carboniferous to Jurassic Highly Fossiliferous (Plants) Bituminous Coal (98% of India's reserves)
Deccan Traps Upper Cretaceous Rare / Intertrappean beds Building stone, bauxite, fertile Black Cotton Soil

Tectonic Cross-Section of Northern India:

Geological Section: Himalayas to Peninsula

sections.title: 3. Physiographic Divisions Linked to Geological History
sections.content:
The geological structure controls the physical features and soils of India, laying the foundation for its agricultural and economic zones.

Agricultural Plain Dynamics
  • Khadar and Bhangar: Newer (Khadar) and older (Bhangar) alluvial belts dictate crop suitability.
  • Karewas: Flat-topped terraces of lake deposits in Kashmir, highly valuable for saffron cultivation.
Industrial & Mineral Base
  • Chotanagpur Plateau: The mineral heart of India, composed of Dharwar and Gondwana structures.
  • Deccan Regur: Fertile black soil supporting the cotton textile hub of Western India.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following rock systems is the primary source of India's metallic mineral wealth, including iron ore, manganese, and gold?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Dharwar System (part of the Archean era) consists of highly metamorphosed sedimentary rocks and is extremely rich in metallic minerals like iron ore, copper, gold, and manganese.

mockTestQuestions.q: With reference to the geological structure of India, which of the following regions contains the oldest rock formations on the subcontinent?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Peninsular Block is a stable shield composed of Archean gneisses and granites, representing the oldest geological division of India.

mockTestQuestions.q: The 'Karewa' formations of Jammu and Kashmir are geologically significant because they are:
opts: Active volcanic craters that erupted in the Pleistocene
Lacustrine deposits of clay and sand famous for saffron cultivation
Glacial moraines containing large reserves of gold
Deep marine sediments containing rich petroleum deposits
mockTestQuestions.sol: Karewas are lacustrine (lake-deposited) clay terrace deposits in the Kashmir Valley, highly valued for growing Saffron (Zafran).

mockTestQuestions.q: In which geological system is approximately 98% of India's coal reserves found?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Gondwana System (Upper Carboniferous to Jurassic) contains almost all of India's coal reserves, formed in freshwater sedimentary basins.

mockTestQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Vindhyan rock system is mostly unfossiliferous and is famous for diamonds and building stones.
2. The Deccan Traps were formed by explosive volcanic eruptions from a single massive stratovolcano.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because the Deccan Traps were formed by quiet fissure eruptions (lava flows) as India passed over the Reunion hotspot, not a stratovolcano.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which geological division of India is considered the youngest in tectonic origin?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Indo-Gangetic plain is the youngest geological region, formed during the Pleistocene epoch by the filling of a foredeep depression with alluvium.

mockTestQuestions.q: The Vindhyan rock system is geologically bounded by which formations to the south?
opts: The Narmada Rift Valley / Satpura Range
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Vindhyan system lies north of the Narmada Rift Valley, which separates it from the Satpura range and the Deccan plateau.

mockTestQuestions.q: The famous diamond mines of Panna (Madhya Pradesh) and Golconda (Telangana) belong to which rock system?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Vindhyan conglomerate beds are the primary source of diamonds in Central India (Panna) and Southern India (Golconda).

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following is the primary soil type derived from the weathering of the Deccan basaltic traps?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Deccan basaltic lava weathered over millions of years to form fertile black clayey soil, ideal for cotton cultivation.

mockTestQuestions.q: The oil reserves of Digboi (Assam) and Ankleshwar (Gujarat) are located in which geological system?
mockTestQuestions.sol: India's petroleum reserves in Assam and Gujarat are found in marine and estuarine sedimentary rocks of the Tertiary system (Oligocene-Miocene).
